claims.text: The target feedstock is AlCrFeNiSi powder intended for miniature additively manufactured components.
A closed-loop machine-learning system can be implemented to adjust laser power, scan speed, and scan path during L-PBF.
Real-time ML control of L-PBF parameters will reduce thermal gradients in AlCrFeNiSi builds.
Large thermal gradients during L-PBF cause residual stresses.
Reduced thermal gradients will produce a more uniform and refined microstructure.
Reduced thermal gradients will lower residual stress and reduce microstructural defects.
The ML algorithm will continuously analyze real-time sensor data to predict the onset of high thermal gradients.
Dynamic adjustment of laser parameters will modulate heating and cooling rates.
Modulating heating and cooling rates will mitigate residual-stress formation and associated microstructural degradation.
ML-controlled components will have fewer microstructural defects than components built using static high-energy parameters.
ML-controlled components will have significantly lower residual thermal stresses than components built using static high-energy parameters.
Lower residual stress and fewer defects will improve strength and ductility.
Conventional fixed, high-energy L-PBF parameters cause rapid thermal cycles and residual-stress buildup.
The proposed approach is applicable to miniature AlCrFeNiSi components under standard laboratory-scale L-PBF conditions.
Effectiveness may vary with powder batch, sensor accuracy, geometry scale, ML-model accuracy, and process-response rate.
A residual-stress reduction of less than 20% relative to the fixed-parameter baseline is offered as an example of failure to demonstrate the predicted reduction.
